title: AI system proves a decades-old quantum computing conjecture

needs.need: Which conjecture was proved, and what it says about the limits of quantum speedups.
needs.accepts: Names the Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture and explains that on random or unstructured yes-or-no inputs a quantum computer can save at most polynomially, not exponentially, many looks at the input compared with an ordinary computer, naming a source. It must not present this as a blanket limit on what quantum computers can do.

example.value: A quantum computer cannot save exponentially many looks on yes-or-no questions unless the input holds a rare pattern; for all but a small fraction of inputs an ordinary computer needs at most polynomially more.
example.source: LavX News, "A proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture" (2026-11-06)

needs.need: Whether anyone outside the company has checked the claim, beyond the machine check.
needs.accepts: Reports that outside peer review of the proof was still pending, or gives a named independent mathematician's assessment of it, and that the paper and Lean formalization are public; names the source.

example.value: PSI published a paper and a public Lean formalization on GitHub, while outside peer review of the proof was still pending.

needs.need: What Lean checks, and why a machine-checked proof is not a test of quantum hardware.
needs.inStory: Lean checked each proof step, reducing the chance of unnoticed logical errors.
needs.accepts: Explains that Lean is a proof assistant that mechanically checks each step of a formally written mathematical argument, as opposed to testing quantum hardware or establishing applications, naming a source.

example.value: Lean is a proof assistant that checks each step in a formal mathematical argument.

needs.need: How the claimed general proof goes beyond the narrower result achieved shortly before it.
needs.accepts: Identifies the August 2026 Stanford result as proving the conjecture's prediction only for quantum algorithms that query their input in a fixed number of parallel rounds, and contrasts it with the claimed general proof, naming the source.

example.value: In August 2026, four Stanford researchers proved there is no exponential speedup on random inputs for algorithms that examine their input in a fixed number of parallel rounds, a special case of the conjecture.

needs.need: What kind of AI system produced the proof, including the model it ran on.
needs.accepts: Reports, attributed to PSI, that its research system ran on its own infrastructure using multiple instances of an unreleased or undisclosed Anthropic model, without presenting PSI's account as independently established.

example.value: PSI said its system ran on its own infrastructure and used multiple instances of an Anthropic model whose name was not disclosed.
example.source: Physical Superintelligence, as reported by TokenPost (2026-11-09) and Business Insider (2026-11-07)

needs.need: Which earlier human mathematical work the AI-produced proof built on.
needs.accepts: Names at least one documented precursor the proof built on, such as Shachar Lovett and Jiapeng Zhang or David Reimer, with a named source.

example.value: The proof built on ideas from Shachar Lovett and Jiapeng Zhang, David Reimer and others.

notNeeded.why: Neither development is a deployed service with an affected population; beneficiary counts would be speculation.
No scheduled review decision or glove rollout is reported; the pending review belongs with the scrutiny need.

notes: The story pairs two unrelated items; the key covers the quantum proof, the story's headline, and leaves the Meta glove to the story. The result concerns input queries, not a blanket limit on quantum computing. Lean acceptance and outside peer review are different things.
